questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis that has clean edges and an indurated base. Inguinal lymphadenopathy is non-tender and rubbery. VDRL is 1:64. Which finding on dark-field microscopy is expected?
questions.exp: The clinical picture describes primary syphilis (Hunterian chancre). Dark-field microscopy of serous exudate from the ulcer demonstrates Treponema pallidum as motile cork-screw (helical) spirochaetes.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer develops grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the right T4 dermatome, preceded by 3 days of burning pain. He is otherwise immunocompetent. What is the drug of choice and recommended duration?
questions.exp: Herpes zoster in an immunocompetent adult is treated with Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days. This dose achieves adequate tissue levels for VZV, which requires higher concentrations than HSV.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman has scaly, hypopigmented macules over the trunk. KOH mount shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (now reclassified under Malassezia species). KOH mount showing short hyphae and round yeast cells — the classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern — is diagnostic.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with leprosy on multi-drug therapy (MDT) develops sudden onset of painful red nodules over the face, trunk, and extremities with fever and joint pains. Biopsy shows erythema nodosum-like histology. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: This is Type 2 lepra reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum — ENL). While thalidomide is very effective, prednisolone (40-60 mg/day) is the first-line treatment, especially in women of childbearing age, due to thalidomide's teratogenicity. MDT should be continued.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin, predominantly on the lower abdomen and thighs. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the basement membrane zone. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense bullae on elderly patients. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ (lamina lucida). Pemphigus shows intercellular IgG. Dermatitis herpetiformis shows granular IgA. Linear IgA shows linear IgA deposits.

questions.q: A 30-year-old butterfly worker develops photosensitivity, a malar rash, oral ulcers, and arthralgia. ANA is positive at 1:640. Anti-dsDNA titre is elevated. Which skin finding is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)?
questions.exp: While malar rash is characteristic, discoid lupus plaques with scarring are a specific criterion for SLE in the ACR classification. However, anti-dsDNA is the most specific antibody. Among skin findings listed, discoid plaques are more specific than the malar rash which can occur in rosacea.

questions.q: A patient presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales over the elbows, knees, and scalp. Biopsy shows parakeratosis, absence of the granular layer, elongated rete ridges, and dilated capillaries in the dermal papillae. What is the Auspitz sign explained by?
questions.exp: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on removal of scales) in psoriasis occurs due to thinning of the suprapapillary epidermis overlying dilated tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae. Scratching removes the thin epidermis exposing these vessels.

questions.q: A 25-year-old shoe factory worker develops erythema and vesicles on both feet sparing the toe webs, after using a new rubber boot. Patch testing is positive to mercaptobenzothiazole. What type of hypersensitivity is this?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity mediated by sensitized T-lymphocytes. Patch testing identifies the culprit allergen after 48-72 hours, confirming T-cell mediated reaction.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with an 8-hour history of widespread urticaria and angioedema following amoxicillin. Blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, pulse 120/min. What is the immediate management?
questions.exp: This is anaphylaxis (urticaria + angioedema + hypotension). Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mL of 1:1000 solution (0.5 mg) in the anterolateral thigh is the immediate, first-line treatment. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts.

questions.q: A leprosy patient presents with sudden weakness of wrist extension and finger extension after 2 weeks of starting MDT. The radial nerve is thickened and tender at the spiral groove. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Start prednisolone 40 mg/day and continue MDT
questions.exp: This is a Type 1 (reversal) reaction with acute neuritis — a medical emergency. High-dose prednisolone (40-60 mg/day, tapered over 6 months) is initiated immediately while MDT is continued. Stopping MDT risks relapse and resistance.

questions.q: A 19-year-old sexually active woman presents with multiple painful vesicles and ulcers on the labia minora, dysuria, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: This is primary genital herpes (HSV-2). Tzanck smear confirms herpetic infection. First episode primary genital herpes is treated with Acyclovir 200 mg 5 times/day for 5-10 days (or 400 mg TDS). Alternatives include valacyclovir 1 g BD.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man has a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectatic vessels on the nasolabial fold present for 2 years. Rolled borders are seen. Biopsy shows palisading basaloid cells with peripheral clefting. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) — the most common skin cancer. Nodular BCC presents as a pearly papule with rolled edges and telangiectasia. Histology shows islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and clefting (retraction artifact). Sun-exposed areas in elderly patients are classic.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man with actinic keratosis over the scalp develops a rapidly growing, firm, indurated plaque with raised everted edges on the right cheek. Biopsy shows dysplastic keratinocytes invading the dermis with keratin pearl formation. What is the most important prognostic factor?
questions.exp: This is squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Perineural invasion is a high-risk feature in SCC associated with local recurrence, nodal metastasis, and poor prognosis. Other high-risk features include depth >2 mm, poor differentiation, and location (lips, ears).

questions.q: A 28-year-old presents with a 2×2 cm irregularly pigmented lesion on the back with variegated colour (brown, black, pink areas), irregular borders, and a diameter of 8 mm. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network. Biopsy confirms melanoma with Breslow thickness 0.8 mm, no ulceration. What is the T stage?
questions.exp: According to AJCC 8th edition, T1a melanoma is <0.8 mm Breslow thickness without ulceration. T1b is <0.8 mm with ulceration OR 0.8-1.0 mm with/without ulceration. This 0.8 mm non-ulcerated melanoma qualifies as T1a.

questions.q: A 32-year-old pregnant woman (28 weeks) develops intensely pruritic, grouped papules and vesicles on the periumbilical area and inner thighs. DIF shows linear C3 deposition at the BMZ. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pemphigoid gestationis (herpes gestationis) presents with periumbilical vesicles in pregnancy. DIF shows linear C3 (and sometimes IgG) at the BMZ — identical to bullous pemphigoid. It is associated with risk of premature delivery and fetal growth restriction.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia, calcinosis cutis, and dysphagia. Which antibody is most specific for her condition?
questions.exp: This is CREST syndrome (limited systemic sclerosis). Anti-centromere antibody is most specific for limited SSc/CREST syndrome. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse SSc. Anti-Jo-1 is for polymyositis. Anti-dsDNA for SLE.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains. Which organism is most commonly responsible?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus (most common) or Streptococcus pyogenes
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is caused by Staphylococcus aureus (most commonly), Streptococcus pyogenes, or both. The classic honey-coloured crust results from serous exudate drying. Gram stain showing gram-positive cocci in chains suggests streptococcal involvement.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 50 cells/μL) presents with extensive molluscum contagiosum lesions (>50 lesions) on the face and neck, some with giant morphology (>5 mm). What does this presentation indicate?
questions.exp: Extensive/giant molluscum contagiosum (>50 lesions or giant lesions >5 mm) in an HIV patient with CD4 <200 indicates severe immunosuppression. It is an AIDS-defining condition. MCV (molluscum contagiosum virus — a poxvirus) proliferates unchecked when cell-mediated immunity fails.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with a history of alcoholism presents with painful, purpuric lesions on the lower limbs. Biopsy shows fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls with neutrophilic infiltration and nuclear dust (leukocytoclasis). C3 and C4 are low. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV) affects small vessels (post-capillary venules). Histology shows fibrinoid necrosis, neutrophilic infiltrate, and karyorrhexis (nuclear dust). Low complement suggests immune complex deposition. LCV is the histological pattern — identifying the underlying cause is essential.

questions.q: During cryotherapy of a wart, the freeze-thaw cycle is applied. What is the recommended freeze time for a periungual wart?
questions.exp: Cryotherapy using liquid nitrogen targets warts by freezing with a 2-3 mm halo of freeze around the lesion. Freeze time is typically 10-30 seconds for periungual warts in a single cycle. Two freeze-thaw cycles are often recommended. Excessive freeze time risks nail matrix damage.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man is started on methotrexate for severe psoriasis. Which baseline investigation is most important before initiating therapy?
opts: Liver function tests and hepatitis B/C serology
questions.exp: Methotrexate is hepatotoxic. Before initiating, baseline LFTs, CBC, renal function, chest X-ray, and hepatitis B/C serology are mandatory. Patients with pre-existing liver disease or active hepatitis B/C require caution or alternative therapy. LFTs and CBC are monitored regularly during treatment.

questions.q: A 27-year-old woman is diagnosed with superficial tinea corporis. Topical clotrimazole is prescribed. She fails to respond after 4 weeks. KOH shows arthroconidia. What is the next step?
opts: Add oral itraconazole 200 mg/day for 2 weeks
Perform fungal culture and sensitivity testing
questions.exp: Treatment failure with topical antifungals warrants fungal culture and sensitivity testing to identify the species and detect resistance. Arthroconidia suggest Trichophyton tonsurans or similar. Empirical oral antifungal escalation without culture risks inappropriate therapy, especially with azole resistance emerging.

questions.q: A patient with multibacillary leprosy is found to have a BI (Bacterial Index) of 4+. What does this mean on the Ridley scale?
questions.exp: The Ridley bacterial index: 1+ = 1-10/100 fields; 2+ = 1-10/10 fields; 3+ = 1-10/field; 4+ = 10-100/field (average 33); 5+ = 100-1000/field; 6+ = >1000/field with globi. BI 4+ indicates heavy bacterial load in multibacillary disease.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a painless chancre on the prepuce followed 6 weeks later by a copper-coloured papular rash on the palms and soles, mucous patches, and condylomata lata. VDRL is 1:128. What is the current stage of syphilis?
questions.exp: Secondary syphilis appears 4-8 weeks after the primary chancre. Classic features include maculopapular rash on palms and soles, condylomata lata (highly infectious flat wart-like lesions), mucous patches, and generalized lymphadenopathy. High VDRL titres (>1:8) support secondary syphilis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman develops a fixed drug eruption on the lips and genitalia (hyperpigmented oval patch that recurs at the same site) after taking cotrimoxazole. The mechanism involves:
opts: Resident CD8+ memory T cells in skin reactivated by drug
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption (FDE) is mediated by intraepidermal CD8+ effector memory T-cells that are 'fixed' at the site of previous reaction. On re-exposure to the drug, these T-cells are reactivated, releasing cytotoxic mediators, explaining the recurrence at identical sites.

questions.q: Dermatoscopy of a pigmented lesion shows a 'starburst pattern' — radial streaks extending symmetrically from the periphery. This pattern is most characteristic of:
questions.exp: Starburst pattern (symmetric radial streaks/pseudopods at the periphery) on dermoscopy is characteristic of Reed nevus (pigmented spindle cell nevus of Reed). This pattern reflects radially arranged melanocytes. Asymmetric starburst pattern raises concern for melanoma.

questions.q: A 10-year-old boy has intensely itchy linear burrows between finger webs, on wrists, and genitalia. Similar symptoms affect other family members. What is the treatment of choice for the entire household?
opts: Permethrin 5% cream applied overnight to the whole body
questions.exp: Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis) presents with pruritic burrows in web spaces. Permethrin 5% cream is the first-line treatment — applied from neck downwards, left overnight (8-12 hours), then washed off. All household and close contacts must be treated simultaneously. Lindane is now avoided due to neurotoxicity.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman develops erythema multiforme (target lesions on palms, forearms, oral mucosa) 10 days after a cold sore. The most common precipitant for recurrent erythema multiforme minor is:
questions.exp: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 or HSV-2) is the most common trigger for recurrent erythema multiforme minor (EMM). HSV-associated EM accounts for >70% of recurrent cases. Mycoplasma and drugs more commonly cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome (EM major with extensive mucosal involvement).

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman undergoes a full-thickness skin graft (FTSG) for a defect on the cheek. What is the primary advantage of FTSG over split-thickness skin graft (STSG) for facial reconstruction?
opts: Less primary contraction and superior cosmetic outcome
questions.exp: FTSG contains both epidermis and full dermis. It undergoes less secondary contraction than STSG (which undergoes more secondary contraction due to less dermis). FTSG provides better colour match, texture, and cosmesis — ideal for facial defects. However, STSG has better take rate in compromised wounds.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with diffuse systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) develops a non-healing ulcer on the fingertip with digital pitting scars. His anti-Scl-70 is positive. Which vascular complication is he at highest risk for?
questions.exp: Diffuse SSc with anti-Scl-70 positivity carries high risk of interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). PAH is a leading cause of death in SSc. Digital ulcers are from obliterative vasculopathy. Annual echocardiography for PAH screening is recommended.
